desc:
The alphabet has k letters, numbered 0 to k - 1. The array pairs lists the allowed ordered neighbours: each entry [x, y] means that letter y may directly follow letter x. Every pair appears at most once, and a pair that is not listed is forbidden.

Count the strings of length n in which every two adjacent letters form an allowed pair. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007. A string of length 1 has no neighbours, so all k single letters are valid.

n = 3, k = 2, pairs = [[0,1],[1,0],[1,1]]  ->  5
  (only the pair "aa" is forbidden: aba, abb, bab, bba, bbb)
n = 5, k = 5, pairs = [[0,1],[1,0],[1,2],[2,0],[2,1],[2,3],[2,4],[3,2],[3,4],[4,0]]  ->  68
constraints: pairs[i] = [x, y] with 0 ≤ x, y < k; all pairs are distinct
hints: For small n a DP works: let ways[c] be the number of valid strings of the current length ending with letter c, and move to the next length through the allowed pairs.
That DP step is a fixed linear map: new = A · old where A is the 0/1 matrix of allowed pairs. Doing it n - 1 times is too slow for n up to a billion.

Apply the matrix n - 1 times with fast exponentiation (square the matrix, multiply it into the vector when the bit is set). With k ≤ 10 each matrix product is only 1,000 multiplications, and about 30 squarings suffice.
editorial: Let M[x][y] = 1 if the pair [x, y] is allowed. The number of valid strings of length n that start with letter x is the number of walks with n - 1 steps starting at x in the directed graph with adjacency matrix M. Counting them step by step is the DP v' = M v starting from the all-ones vector (a string of length 1 is always valid), so the vector after n - 1 steps is Mn-1 · 1 and the answer is the sum of its entries.

Because powers of M commute, Mn-1 can be applied with binary exponentiation: loop over the bits of n - 1, multiply the current vector by the current matrix when the bit is set, and square the matrix. That costs O(k3 log n) time (about 30 · 1,000 multiplications here) and O(k2) space, everything modulo 1,000,000,007.
The second example is the well-known vowel rule set (a is followed only by e, e by a or i, i by anything except i, o by i or u, u only by a), which gives 68 strings of length 5.
